beats: Hook: to fix a qubit you need to know what went wrong, but looking at it destroys it. What can you ask that reveals the error and nothing else? (line_qc_synd_hand_on_flap; reuse line_qc_parity_open_flaps, QC06-02: lifting the flaps ruins the pair.) Cast as in QC08-01: the keeper (the code) and the imp (the noise). The quantum hallway: the plates now keep their flaps closed (lifting a flap = measuring a data qubit); the two bulbs between neighbours are the helper qubits, QC06-02's plant (reuse line_qc_parity_three_switches). Convention for QC08: a bulb lights when its two switches disagree (its helper reads 1, eigenvalue -1), as QC06-02's plant beat says ("a lit bulb points at the odd switch"); QC06-02's hook line says "lights when they agree": make the two films use one convention.
Why the qubits cannot simply be measured (14:14-17:10; Q24-09 11:06-13:04; clip Q25-10 16:30-17:10 "you just measure the error, not the data"; tape Q24-09 p7).

Two helper qubits, four syndromes (17:10-24:53; tape Q24-09 p8): left bulb only -> switch 1, both -> switch 2, right bulb only -> switch 3, none -> no error (line_qc_synd_read_bulbs: the left bulb lit, the keeper points at the first plate without opening anything; the code letters the syndrome table).
A lookup-table decoder (25:26-26:22): the fix is a flip made without looking, an X on qubit 1 with nothing measured (line_qc_synd_blind_fix).
It assumes perfect checks (26:22-26:56; Q24-09 23:29-24:30): what if a helper itself fails? (line_qc_synd_bulb_prank) The answer is QC08-08.

Two flips swap alpha and beta (27:26-28:47): switches 1 and 2 flipped light the right bulb, which points at the innocent switch 3; the "fix" completes the damage: a logical error (line_qc_synd_wrong_fix; reuse line_qc_vote_two_flipped, its classical twin).

The shortcut (29:05-35:01): push the X error through the CNOTs; an error on a data qubit travels along its wires into the helpers it is wired to, and the middle switch is wired to both bulbs, so it lights both (line_qc_synd_wall_wiring3; the code draws the circuit). Why it works (35:08-36:01; clip "we never measure anything associated with alpha and beta"): only parities are read (line_qc_synd_wall_wiring3 again).

Stabilizers (36:27-42:17; tape Q24-09 p12): the good state is a +1 eigenstate of Z1Z2 and Z2Z3, an error flips one or both to -1; minimal generators; k = n - m (3 - 2 = 1 logical qubit). Collapse happens only if the state is not an eigenstate (Q24-09 38:15-38:42, clip): a question whose answer is already settled changes nothing (pen work, no drawing).

The stabilizer measurement is QC06-02's helper circuit, H, controlled-U, H, with only the helper read (42:17-49:31; tape Q24-09 p14; reuse line_qc_parity_wall_wiring). Avoid Q24-09 16:10-18:28 and 39:09-41:08 (student questions: her answers only).
Cover (line_qc_cover_08_02; for the X post and thumbnails, not a film beat): three closed flaps, one lit bulb; the keeper points at the culprit plate, the imp tiptoes away caught.

drawings.prompt: A long plain hallway wall seen straight from the front. Along it, at hand height, three identical wall plates sit in a row, evenly spaced, and each is covered by a small closed hinged flap so its switch cannot be seen. From the ceiling hang two bare light bulbs on short cords: one exactly halfway between the first and second plate, the other exactly halfway between the second and third plate (a lit bulb is an empty bulb outline with short straight rays around it; an unlit bulb is a plain empty bulb outline). Both bulbs are unlit. The keeper (an invented young woman with a simple round face and dot eyes, chin-length straight hair held back on one side by a single plain hair clip, a plain one-piece zip-up work overall with the sleeves rolled up and a small torch clipped to its chest pocket, and sturdy work boots) stands in front of the middle plate with her fingertips under the edge of its closed flap, about to lift it, and freezes: she looks back over her shoulder towards the viewer with a worried face, eyebrows raised, one small drop of sweat at her temple. The imp (an invented small mischievous creature, about knee-high to an adult: a round, bean-shaped body, a simple round face with dot eyes and a wide cheeky grin, two big pointed ears sticking out sideways, thin arms and legs, small three-fingered hands and a thin curly tail; drawn in clean outline only: no fur, no horns, no claws, no teeth) sits on the floor at the right, leaning back on his hands, watching with a cheeky grin.
